transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-12-01
- Start: 15:00 PST
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jenna Ortiz (BrightScale Head of ML Infra), Marcus Li (BrightScale Platform Eng), Priya Reddy (BrightScale SecOps)

Summary: brief review of current perf pain points and a hands-on walkthrough of tuning knobs to hit BrightScale's throughput SLOs while keeping 95p latency under 400ms.

[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll hand over to Samir to kick off the deep dive. we wanted to focus on your continuous batching concerns and some concrete scheduler knobs that have helped other on-prem customers.

[00:22] Samir Patel: Hi all, thanks Alex. Jenna, Marcus — could you remind me real quick of your topology? I have notes you have on-prem kubernetes with NVLink GPUs, and you're running the model as a private deployment behind a VPC gateway?

[00:40] Jenna Ortiz: yeah that's right. We're 3 racks of A100-ish machines, NVLink enabled, k8s cluster, but we do a mix of pods and baremetal for performance. we sit behind a customer-managed LB, and we can't route outbound to Redwood in prod for security reasons, so the plan is for a private deployment with a small control plane connection.

[01:05] Samir Patel: understood. that's a common setup. quick qual: what's your traffic shape? p50/p95 sequence length and RPS?

[01:17] Marcus Li: Traffic right now is spiky — we have bursts from the product UX tests. p50 seq length ~45 tokens, p95 ~210 tokens, steady around 120 rps at peak bursts. goal is to sustain 200 rps for 10s windows with 95p latency under 400ms.

[01:42] Samir Patel: ok that helps. so primary levers are: continuous batching windows, max_num_seqs (sequence packing per batch), token limits per request, and KV cache policies. We'll walk through each and show example numbers.

[02:05] Samir Patel: first, continuous batching. by default Redwood runtime uses a continuous batching loop that waits up to a small time quantum to aggregate requests. increasing max batch duration helps throughput but hurts tail latency. for your profile I'd recommend lowering batch wait to 8ms with an adaptive fallback to 30ms under low load. that allows your short requests to not sit too long but still pack during spikes.

[02:45] Jenna Ortiz: when you say pack, that's sequence packing into the same batch, right? how does that interact with max_num_seqs?

[02:54] Samir Patel: exact. max_num_seqs is the scheduler knob that caps how many sequences we can pack in a single forward. with your 210-token p95, we suggested max_num_seqs=8 on A100 to avoid memory oversubscribe. Combined with dynamic per-seq token limit, we can reduce OOMs. For example packing eight 200-token sequences is different than eight 45-token sequences. runtime estimates cumulative tokens.

[03:24] Marcus Li: hmm ok, memory peaks are our main worry. we saw OOMs on initial runs when we used seq_pack enabled. is there an auto-throttle?

[03:33] Samir Patel: yes, there is. runtime exposes scheduler hooks: soft_max_tokens and hard_max_tokens. soft_max triggers earlier batching flushes, hard_max will refuse new sequences. we usually set soft_max to 85% of GPU mem reserved for model, and hard_max at 95%. Also set a per-request token_limit param so client side truncates or rejects very long prompts.

[04:05] Priya Reddy: on the security side, anything about KV cache we should be aware of? we need to guarantee no sensitive context persists beyond the call, ideally per-request encryption and evictions.

[04:18] Samir Patel: good point. KV cache is in-GPU memory by default and is ephemeral per model instance. for private deployments we support explicit eviction APIs and TTLs, and Redwood can be configured to zero out caches on session termination. there's also an option to use encrypted swap for very long sequences but that hurts latency.

[04:44] Jenna Ortiz: you mentioned TTLs — how long do caches keep context during a stream?

[04:49] Samir Patel: default is 20 minutes for cached prefixes, but you can set it to session-only. for privacy you'll want session-only and explicit eviction on disconnect. we'll include config snippet.

[05:05] Samir Patel: next, quantization. moving to 4-bit quantization gets you memory headroom to increase max_num_seqs but may change token quality slightly for our models. For your use-case (lots of short answers), we typically recommend starting with 8-bit dynamic and test 4-bit on a subset of traffic in a canary. that gives about ~1.8x throughput improvement for large seq packing.

[05:36] Marcus Li: do you have numbers for latency difference when using 4-bit vs fp16?

[05:41] Samir Patel: ballpark: fp16 single-seq p95 on A100 ~220ms. 8-bit quantized p95 ~200ms thanks to cache fit and batching; 4-bit is similar or slightly faster but can add conversion overhead in some kernels so p95 ~190-210ms depending on kernel set. main gain is capacity for more concurrent sequences per GPU.

[06:08] Alex Kim: also note that quantization can affect output determinism — good to run evals. Samir will share our quantization report and eval prompts.

[06:21] Samir Patel: moving on to scheduler knobs we often tune: batch_wait_ms, max_num_seqs, soft_max_tokens, hard_max_tokens, token_limit_per_request, and early_batch_fill_threshold. we can provide recommended defaults for A100 NVLink with your workload.

[06:40] Jenna Ortiz: about token_limit_per_request — we have long system prompts occasionally; is truncation recommended or should we fail?

[06:48] Samir Patel: depends on your app. we recommend soft truncation with a warning and a logs-only rejection for very long prompts initially. i.e., set token_limit 1024 and return 413-like error when >2048 so clients can be updated. trunking is lossy.

[07:10] [08:12] Marcus Li: there's a part I wanted to dig deeper — continuous batching and the scheduler interactions under bursty traffic; does Redwood do request prioritization?

[07:22] Samir Patel: yes we have fair-share and priority tag routing. for instance you can reserve 20% of slots for low-latency channels. the scheduler will attempt to pack low-priority sequences when they don't affect reserved slots. so in your case we could reserve a small steady pool for the UI hot path and let background jobs use remaining capacity.

[07:48] Jenna Ortiz: can you show the config file?

[07:52] Samir Patel: sure i pasted a sample in the meeting chat, but i'll share a cleaned version after. key sections: scheduler: { batch_wait_ms: 8, max_num_seqs: 8, soft_max_tokens: 85_percent, hard_max_tokens: 95_percent, reserved_slots: { ui: 0.2 } } (note: chat transcription mangled curly braces).

[08:18] Priya Reddy: a couple security questions — KMS integration on Private, and audit logs for cache eviction.

[08:25] Alex Kim: we support AWS KMS and customer HSM via PKCS11 for Private. audit logs for cache and session lifecycle are emitted to your configured syslog or S3 bucket with integrity hashes. we'll send SOC2 artifacts as part of the security package.

[08:42] Jenna Ortiz: good. on networking, if we do Private there's egress constraints; can Redwood's agent run in an airgapped mode with periodic signed snapshots?

[08:53] Samir Patel: yes — private on-prem mode supports offline control plane with signed manifests. that adds complexity for upgrades but it's supported. we've done similar for a fintech customer.

[09:05] [09:20] Marcus Li: ok can we look at a concrete bench plan? what do you need from us?

[09:28] Samir Patel: we need a representative traffic trace (timestamps, seq lengths, per-request metadata) and a window for 48-hour run. we'll deploy a small pilot runtime with the recommended scheduler knobs and run with metrics exported to your prometheus. we'll compare throughput, p50/p95 latency, and GPU mem/activation curves.

[09:54] Jenna Ortiz: i can export traces. small ask: do you require any kernel-level changes or can this run on our existing runtime containers?

[10:03] Samir Patel: it runs on our runtime container. if you want to keep your own runtime we can provide a binary. we do need profile hooks enabled and permission to collect perf counters.

[10:15] Alex Kim: we'll also provide a set of eval prompts to check quality across quantization levels.

[10:22] Samir Patel: quick note on max_num_seqs interplay with KV cache: if you pack many independent conversations, the KV cache size grows linearly. to mitigate this we do prefix dedupe and a shared cache keyed by prompt fingerprint. that reduces memory but can slightly increase miss penalty.

[10:46] Marcus Li: can you elaborate on prefix dedupe? sounds risky for privacy.

[10:50] Samir Patel: good callout. prefix dedupe only applies to non-sensitive, public system prompts and can be disabled. for private prompt data we don't dedupe. we can set a policy to only dedupe for model housekeeping tokens not customer text.

[11:10] Jenna Ortiz: what about cost tradeoffs? if we increase max_num_seqs and pack more, our cost per token goes down but latency could go up for some requests?

[11:20] Alex Kim: correct — it's a utilization vs tail-latency trade. for BrightScale's goal to sustain high throughput with acceptable 95p, our suggested pattern is reserved slots for hot paths + aggressive packing for batch jobs, and use quantization to expand capacity. we'll include a cost model spreadsheet.

[11:40] Priya Reddy: one more security item — do you support per-tenant KMS keys for encrypted swap?

[11:47] Samir Patel: yes we can mount tenant-specific keys. encrypted swap is optional and slower; only recommended if you have very large sequences.

[12:05] Alex Kim: ok let's recap and action items. Samir, you'll share scheduler config and the quant report. Jenna will send traffic trace. Alex to send pricing and pilot terms.

[12:20] Jenna Ortiz: makes sense. any blockers from our side? only that we need to confirm an upgrade freeze window for the pilot.

[12:29] Marcus Li: i'll own the bench window scheduling.

[12:34] [12:50] Alex Kim: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule.

End of transcript.
